name: Ares Management Corporation

profile.description: Ares Management is a global alternative investment manager focused on private credit, with additional platforms in private equity, real estate, infrastructure, and secondaries. In Q3 2026 it reported fee-related earnings of $524.2M, after-tax realized income of $449.6M, and more than $31B of gross capital commitments, while GAAP net income attributable to Ares was $85.3M [1]. GAAP revenue grew from $1.76B in FY2020 to $6.47B in FY2025 [2]. The stock sold off sharply in 2026 on investor fears about AI disruption to software borrowers in private credit portfolios [3][4].

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): Ares has scaled from a credit specialist into a multi-strategy alternatives platform spanning private equity, real estate, infrastructure, and secondaries, lifting GAAP revenue at a 29.7% CAGR from $1.76B (FY2020) to $6.47B (FY2025) [2]. AI Deployment (1/2): Ares evaluated 160 AI use cases in 2025 and has 25 actively deployed across front, middle, and back office, including AI-assisted investment memos, but has not quantified savings or AI revenue [3]. Market Share (1/2): A top-tier private credit manager raising $31B+ in a single quarter, but no fetched data shows it gaining share against Apollo, Blackstone, or Blue Owl [1]. Pipeline (1/2): Management points to 'substantial embedded growth' from capital raised but not yet earning fees and expects another record fundraising year, without dated product launches [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): FMP reports no R&D expense [2].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Ares frames its purpose around being a trusted capital partner that generates consistent returns for investors and supports businesses across market cycles; it is clear and credible for a credit manager but not distinctive beyond the obvious. Community Impact (0/2): This research found no specific charitable programs or dollar amounts; ESG content in the 10-K filings covers risk disclosures (anti-ESG state laws, DEI scrutiny, climate and human-rights reputational risk) rather than community investment [5]. Employee Retention (0/2): No turnover or tenure data were found. Insider Buying (0/2): No net insider buying in the last 12 months was identified.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on 10 Dividend-sleeve metrics (12 weight units). Strengths: forward P/E 18.2x (1.0), a 29.7% five-year revenue CAGR (1.0), 11 consecutive full years of dividends since the 2014 IPO (2x, 1.0), and a 22.9% five-year dividend CAGR ($1.60 in 2020 to $4.48 in 2025, 2x, 1.0) [2][6][7]. Middling: ROE 10.3% (0.69), D/E 172% (0.55), six consecutive years of annual dividend growth since 2020 (0.60), and profit margin 8.7% (0.43). Weak: GAAP revenue fell 18.7% YoY as carried-interest income swung (0.04), and the GAAP payout ratio of 444% scores 0, since the $5.17 TTM dividend is paid from fee-related and realized income rather than GAAP EPS of $1.90 [6][7]. Weighted sum 8.32/12 = 6.9, rounded to 7. Liquidity passes: $128.15 x 2.24M shares (~$287M/day) [6].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (6/9): Originating, structuring, and workout of private loans relies on relationships, proprietary deal flow, and long-dated locked-up capital that AI does not replace, and CEO Michael Arougheti called market AI fears 'odd' [3]. The market disagrees enough to matter: the stock fell about 32% in a single quarter through March 2026 on worries about AI-disrupted software borrowers, although management says software is about 12% of the direct lending book and a study cited on the Q1 2026 call put only about 1% of the portfolio in the high-risk category [3][4]. AI Opportunity (0/1): Ares does not report quantified AI-attributable revenue; its 25 deployed AI use cases are internal productivity tools [3].

infinite_game.summary: Ares has the continuity Sinek respects (co-founder Michael Arougheti still leads) and a long record of patient credit investing through cycles. But its stated purpose is a capital-markets value proposition rather than a Just Cause, its growth is measured in AUM and fundraising records, and its dividend now exceeds GAAP earnings. It plays a longer game than most asset managers, but the scorecard is still finite.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Ares speaks of being a trusted partner that delivers consistent returns and supports businesses through cycles, but the story management tells investors is built on fundraising ($31B+ in Q3 2026), fee-related earnings, and AUM growth, not an idealistic future state [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Co-founder leadership continuity and partnership-style economics point to a stable organization [3], but no retention data or employee-sentiment evidence was found to support a high-trust rating.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Management commentary focuses on defending its portfolio against AI fears and on fundraising scale; no evidence was found of Ares framing peers such as Apollo or Blackstone as rivals that push it to improve [3][4].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Ares has broadened from a credit-focused manager into private equity, real estate, infrastructure, and secondaries, with revenue up roughly 3.7x since 2020 [2]. These are adjacent expansions of the same fee-earning model rather than a reinvention.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): During the 2026 AI-driven selloff, Arougheti publicly defended the private credit model and said Ares saw a strong 2026 deal pipeline, continuing to deploy capital rather than retrench [3]. That counter-cyclical stance is real, but no pattern of sacrificing near-term earnings was found.

investment_thesis: Ares remains a fundraising machine: it raised more than $31B of gross commitments in Q3 2026, generated $524.2M of fee-related earnings and $449.6M of after-tax realized income, and expects another record fundraising year, with substantial capital raised but not yet earning fees [1]. The 2026 AI-driven selloff (down about 22% year to date per TIKR) leaves the stock at 18.2x forward earnings with a 4.0% yield, while management estimates only about 1% of the portfolio is at high AI-disruption risk [4][6][7]. Its dividend has compounded at 22.9% a year since 2020 [6].
thesis_continued: The bear case starts with GAAP earnings quality. Q3 2026 GAAP net income attributable to Ares was just $85.3M, TTM GAAP revenue fell 18.7%, EPS growth was -77%, and the $5.17 TTM dividend is about 4.4x GAAP EPS, so the payout depends on fee and realized income holding up [1][6][7]. Leverage is meaningful (D/E 172%, net debt about 6.2x EBITDA), and private credit faces a cycle test if AI or a slowdown impairs software and middle-market borrowers [7]. At 7.3x book and 59x trailing GAAP earnings, a fundraising slowdown would leave little valuation support [7].
key_catalysts: Deployment of capital raised but not yet earning fees, which management says provides substantial embedded growth in management fees and FRE [1]
Another record fundraising year, extending the $31B+ of gross commitments raised in Q3 2026 [1]
Easing AI-disruption fears if software borrowers keep performing, supporting management's view that only about 1% of the portfolio is high-risk [3][4]
key_risks: Credit losses in the direct lending book, where software is about 12% of exposure and AI disruption could impair borrowers faster than expected [3]
Dividend coverage risk: the $5.17 TTM dividend is about 4.4x GAAP EPS of $1.90, so any decline in realized income or FRE would pressure the payout [7]
Fundraising slowdown or a private credit repricing that compresses fee growth while leverage stays elevated (D/E 172%, net debt/EBITDA about 6.2x) [6][7]
